back: The movement of sucrose and amino acids in the phloem from sources to sinks.

front: What is a **source**? Give two examples.
back: A part of a plant that releases sucrose or amino acids into the phloem, e.g. a mature leaf in the light, a sprouting potato tuber.

front: What is a **sink**? Give three examples.
back: A part of a plant that takes sucrose or amino acids out of the phloem to use or store, e.g. roots, shoot tips, developing fruits and seeds, storage organs being filled.

front: In which direction does phloem carry food?
back: In any direction, up or down, from sources to sinks (xylem carries water upwards only).

front: How can a sweet potato storage root be both a sink and a source? (Supplement)
back: Sink while filling: it takes in sucrose and stores starch. Source when sprouting: starch is converted to sucrose and sent to the new shoots.

front: Why is a young leaf a sink but a mature leaf a source?
back: A young, growing leaf uses more sucrose than it makes, so it imports it; a mature leaf makes more than it uses and exports it.

front: Why is carbohydrate transported as sucrose, not starch?
back: Sucrose is soluble, so it can be carried in solution in the phloem; starch is insoluble.
Removing a complete ring of bark (containing the phloem) from a woody stem, leaving the xylem (wood) intact.

front: Effects of ring-barking a tree trunk
back: Sucrose builds up above the ring, which swells; the roots receive no sucrose, cannot respire and die; then the tree dies. Leaves stay green at first because the xylem still carries water.

front: How do aphids provide evidence that phloem carries sugar?
back: Aphids feed from the phloem; sap flowing from their mouthparts (left in the stem) contains sucrose and amino acids.
